title: Welcome and Table of Contents
summary: What SS1 Literature in English First Term is about, how to use the notes, and a map of every unit.

p: Literature is the art of words. In this subject you read stories, poems and plays, you learn how writers create their effects, and you learn to explain what you think and to support it with evidence from the text.

In First Term you learn what literature is and why it matters, how to appreciate a text (theme, plot, setting, style, tone and mood), the main figures of speech, and the three genres: prose, poetry and drama. Then you study your first set text, Shakespeare's tragedy Antony and Cleopatra.

Read each unit slowly. When a unit gives an example, try to think of your own. At the end of every unit are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit. Essay assignments from the school scheme of work are given in the 'Try it yourself' box of the unit, so you can practise writing.

title: What Is Literature? Its Functions
summary: The meaning of literature, its key characteristics, oral and written literature, and six functions: to entertain, to teach, to mirror society, to criticise society, to preserve culture and to develop feelings.

p: In its widest meaning, literature is all the writing of a particular culture, language or time. In the narrower sense used in this subject, Literature (with a capital L) is imaginative or creative writing that has artistic value and speaks to people everywhere. It explores the human condition, ideas, feelings and experiences through language that is carefully crafted and meant to do more than just give information. A shopping list or a simple news report is writing, but it is not usually called literature.

Imaginative: it comes from the imagination (fiction, poetry, drama). Artistic: language is used skilfully and beautifully, with figures of speech, rhythm and shape. Universal: its themes (love, death, conflict, justice) matter to people in all cultures and times. Open to interpretation: different readers can find different meanings in the same text.
Literature can be oral (passed on by word of mouth: folktales, myths, legends, proverbs, songs) or written (recorded in text).
1. To entertain: literature gives pleasure and escape. The Romans called this the 'sweet' (dulce) side of literature.
2. To educate and inform: literature teaches about the world, cultures, history and human behaviour, and gives moral lessons. This is the 'useful' (utile) side.
3. To mirror society (reflective function): it shows the values, beliefs, problems, vices and virtues of the society in which it was written.
4. To criticise society (corrective function): authors use stories, poems and plays to expose injustice and corruption, as in satire, and to urge change.
5. To preserve culture: literature is an archive of a people's language, myths, customs and history, handed from one generation to the next.
6. Emotional and psychological development: by living through characters' feelings, we understand our own and other people's, and we grow in empathy.

title: Why We Study Literature
summary: The benefits of studying literature: critical thinking, better language, empathy, a wider worldview and an understanding of history and culture.

sections.h: A part of a rounded education
p: Studying literature does much more than prepare you for an examination. It builds skills and attitudes that you will use for the rest of your life.

1. Critical thinking: a literary text is complex and sometimes ambiguous. To understand it you must read the words carefully, look for patterns, form an opinion (an interpretation) and support it with evidence from the text.
2. Better language and communication: wide reading adds to your vocabulary, shows you how good writers build sentences and shows the power of well-chosen words. Your own speaking and writing improve.
3. Empathy: literature lets you 'step into the shoes' of people from other backgrounds, places and times. This 'vicarious experience' helps you to understand human nature.
4. A broader worldview: it takes you beyond your own limited experience to new ideas, beliefs and ways of seeing the world.
5. Understanding history and culture: a novel or a play can show what a war or a social system felt like for the people who lived through it, which a history textbook cannot do in the same way.
Reading closely, analysing, interpreting, comparing texts, arguing a point with evidence, writing clearly and respecting other people's views are all skills practised in Literature-in-English.

title: Literary Appreciation: Theme, Plot and Setting
summary: What literary appreciation is, and three of its elements: theme, plot (with the five parts of a plot) and setting.

p: Literary appreciation is the process of analysing, understanding and judging a work of literature to find out how and why it creates its effects. It is more than just liking a book. It involves analysis (breaking the text into parts such as plot, character and setting), interpretation (deciding what it means and what the writer wants to say) and evaluation (judging its artistic quality and impact).

The theme is the central idea or message of a text: a truth about life or human nature that the writer explores. A theme is not a single word such as 'love'. It is a statement about that word, such as 'Love can destroy as well as heal' or 'True love needs sacrifice'. A text can have one major theme and several minor ones.

The plot is the series of connected events that make up the story: the 'what happens'. A typical plot has five parts (called Freytag's pyramid). Exposition: the beginning, which introduces the characters, setting and first conflict. Rising action: complications and obstacles that build tension. Climax: the highest point of tension, the turning point where the conflict comes to a head. Falling action: events after the climax, as tension drops and the results unfold. Resolution (denouement): the end, when the conflict is settled and a new normal is set up.

p: Setting is the time and place in which the story happens. Physical setting is the location (a city, a jungle, a room). Temporal setting is the time (the 19th century, wartime, one day). Social or cultural setting covers the customs, values and rules of the society in the story. Setting is important because it can affect the plot, influence how characters behave and create the mood.

title: Literary Appreciation: Style, Tone and Mood
summary: Style (diction, syntax, devices), tone as the writer's attitude and mood as the feeling created in the reader.

p: Style is the writer's own way of using language: how a writer writes, not what the writer writes about. It includes diction (the choice of words: formal or informal, simple or complex, concrete or abstract), syntax (how words are arranged into sentences: long flowing sentences or short choppy ones) and the use of literary devices such as metaphors, similes and imagery.

Tone is the writer's or narrator's attitude to the subject or the audience. It is shown through diction, events and the way characters are described. Examples of tone: serious, humorous, cynical, sarcastic, optimistic, critical, nostalgic, formal.

Mood is the general feeling or atmosphere that the text creates in the reader. Setting is a main tool for creating mood: 'a dark and stormy night' gives a gloomy, tense mood. Examples of mood: suspenseful, joyful, mysterious, terrifying, peaceful, melancholic.

title: Figures of Speech I: Simile, Metaphor, Irony, Personification, Oxymoron
summary: The meaning of figures of speech and five of them with definitions, functions and examples, including the three types of irony.

p: Figures of speech (also called literary or rhetorical devices) are words or expressions used in a non-literal, imaginative way to create a special effect, to stress a point or to make language vivid and memorable. They let writers 'paint pictures with words' and say more than the dictionary meanings (denotation) of the words.

A simile makes a direct comparison between two different things using 'like' or 'as'. Examples: 'He is as brave as a lion.' 'The memory faded like a dream.' It makes a description vivid by linking something unfamiliar to something familiar.

A metaphor says that one thing IS another, without 'like' or 'as'. Examples: 'He is a lion in the fight.' 'All the world's a stage' (Shakespeare). 'She has a heart of stone.' A metaphor is a stronger comparison, because it makes the reader see the likeness more deeply.

Irony is a contrast between what is expected and what actually is. There are three main types. Verbal irony (like sarcasm): a speaker says the opposite of what they mean, for example saying 'Lovely weather we're having' in a hurricane. Situational irony: the result of a situation is the opposite of what was expected, for example a fire station burning down. Dramatic irony: the audience or reader knows something important that a character does not. In Romeo and Juliet, the audience knows that Juliet has only taken a sleeping drug, but Romeo believes she is dead. This creates suspense.

Personification gives human qualities, feelings or actions to objects, animals or ideas. Examples: 'The wind whispered through the trees.' 'Justice is blind.' 'The sun smiled down on us.' It makes abstract ideas easier to picture.

An oxymoron puts two opposite or contradictory words side by side to create a new, complex meaning. Examples: 'jumbo shrimp', 'living dead', 'deafening silence', 'a bittersweet memory'. It is used for dramatic effect or to show mixed feelings.

The lesson plan says that in Romeo and Juliet the audience knows Romeo is only sleeping, but Juliet thinks he is dead. It is the other way round: Juliet takes the drug and appears dead, and Romeo, who does not know the plan, believes she is dead and kills himself.

title: Figures of Speech II: Euphemism, Alliteration, Hyperbole, Allusion, Assonance, Paradox, Repetition
summary: Seven more figures of speech with definitions, functions, examples and the differences between alliteration and assonance and between oxymoron and paradox.

p: A euphemism replaces a harsh or blunt expression with a mild, indirect one. Examples: 'He passed away' (instead of 'He died'); 'She is between jobs' (instead of 'unemployed'); 'The company is downsizing' (instead of 'sacking workers'). It softens a harsh truth or is used to be polite, and sometimes to mislead.

Alliteration is the repetition of the same initial consonant sound in a series of words. Examples: 'She sells seashells by the seashore.' 'The wicked witch of the West.' 'Pride and Prejudice.' It creates rhythm and makes a phrase easy to remember.
Hyperbole is extreme exaggeration for emphasis or humour, not meant literally. Examples: 'I'm so hungry I could eat a horse.' 'I've told you a million times.' 'This bag weighs a ton.'

An allusion is an indirect reference to a well-known person, place, event or work (from the Bible, mythology, history or Shakespeare). It adds meaning by linking the text to a wider culture and depends on the reader's shared knowledge. Examples: 'He was a real Samaritan about it' (the Good Samaritan); 'She had a Mona Lisa smile'; 'He has an Achilles' heel' (a weak point, from Greek myth).

Assonance is the repetition of vowel sounds inside words in a line. Examples: 'The rain in Spain falls mainly on the plain' (the long 'ay' sound); 'Try to light the fire.' It creates internal rhyme and music. Alliteration is about the first consonant sounds; assonance is about vowel sounds inside words.

A paradox is a statement that seems to contradict itself or to be absurd but, when you think about it, holds a deeper truth. Examples: 'You must be cruel to be kind.' 'War is peace' (George Orwell's 1984). 'This is the beginning of the end.' An oxymoron is two words ('living dead'); a paradox is a whole statement or idea ('The child is father of the man').

Repetition is the deliberate repeating of a word, phrase or sentence for effect: emphasis, rhythm, suspense or to stress a theme. Examples: 'Rage, rage against the dying of the light' (Dylan Thomas). In Martin Luther King Jr's speech the repeated 'I have a dream' at the start of clauses is a kind of repetition called anaphora.
